11730:
Overarching describes something that is so broad and important that it covers, includes, and connects everything else beneath it — like a master idea, a top-level goal, or a grand framework that all other things belong to or serve.

When you call something "overarching," you are saying three things about it at once:

  1. It is the most important. It sits at the top of the hierarchy.
  2. It is the most comprehensive. It is wide enough to include everything else under it.
  3. Everything else serves it or falls under it. The smaller things don't exist independently — they are parts of this bigger thing.

Think of a physical arch — like the curved stone arch of a bridge or a grand doorway. An arch curves up and over everything beneath it. It shelters, connects, and contains what is under it. The word "overarching" borrows exactly this image. When something is described as overarching, picture it as a giant arch stretching above everything else, with all the smaller pieces sitting comfortably underneath it.

Imagine a company that wants to:

  • Increase sales
  • Improve customer service
  • Cut costs
  • Hire better employees

Now imagine there is one single big goal that all of these smaller goals are working toward: "To become the most trusted company in the world."

That big goal is the overarching goal. Every smaller goal — sales, service, costs, hiring — exists in order to serve that one big goal. They all live under it.

You would say: "The company's overarching goal is to become the most trusted company in the world."

• "The overarching theme of the novel is the search for identity."

Every character, scene, and plot twist in the book connects back to this one grand theme. It is the idea that covers the whole story.

  • "The overarching principle of the legal system is fairness."

Every individual law, rule, and courtroom procedure is meant to serve this one highest principle.

  • "The government set an overarching strategy for fighting poverty."

All individual policies — housing, education, healthcare — are parts of this one master strategy.

  • "She had one overarching concern: the safety of her children."

Everything else she worried about was secondary to this one big concern.
What Nouns Does It Typically Describe?

"Overarching" almost always appears before abstract nouns — big, important concepts. The most common combinations are:

  • Overarching goal / aim / objective
  • Overarching theme
  • Overarching principle / rule
  • Overarching framework / structure
  • Overarching strategy / plan
  • Overarching question / concern
  • Overarching narrative / story

You would rarely use it to describe a physical or concrete object (not "an overarching chair"). It belongs to the world of ideas, plans, and purposes.
How Is It Different From Similar Words?

This is where many learners get confused. Here is a clear breakdown:

"Overarching" vs. "main" or "primary":
These just mean "most important." But "overarching" goes further — it means the thing doesn't just rank first; it contains and governs all the others.

"The main goal is to win the championship." → It's the top priority, but it doesn't necessarily say anything about how the other goals relate to it.

"The overarching goal is to win the championship." → Winning is the master goal, and every other goal — training harder, staying healthy, building teamwork — exists in service of this one.

"Overarching" vs. "overall":
"Overall" simply means "when everything is considered together." It doesn't imply a hierarchy or a governing framework.

"The overall result was good." → A summary of things added together.

"The overarching goal was good." → The master goal that guided everything.

"Overarching" vs. "central":
"Central" means most important or at the core. But "overarching" adds the sense of being above and covering everything, not just being at the center.
The Key Feeling of the Word

If you had to capture the spirit of "overarching" in a sentence, it would be this:

"Everything else is a smaller piece of this one big thing."

Whenever you read or hear "overarching," your brain should immediately ask: "What are the smaller things underneath it?" Because an overarching idea always implies that there are smaller ideas, goals, or elements that live under its canopy.

Use "overarching" when you want to show that one big idea, goal, or principle governs or contains a whole set of smaller ones. It is a word that signals hierarchy and comprehensiveness at the same time.

Do not use it just to mean "very important" or "big." Something can be very important without being overarching. The right moment to use it is specifically when you want to say: "This thing is the master-level concept. Everything else is subordinate to it."

It is widely used in formal writing — academic essays, business strategy, policy documents, and literary analysis — though it also appears naturally in everyday speech.
11731: To overawe someone means to impress or intimidate them so powerfully — through your authority, skill, reputation, beauty, or sheer presence — that they feel deeply overwhelmed and unable to act freely, speak up, or resist you. The person who is overawed is essentially frozen in a state of wonder mixed with a kind of fear or submission.

Before you can fully grasp overawe, you need to feel the weight of the word awe sitting inside it.

Awe is that breathtaking feeling you get when you encounter something so grand, so powerful, or so extraordinary that it stops you in your tracks. Think of standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon for the first time, or watching a once-in-a-generation musician perform live. You feel small. You feel stunned. You feel deep, almost reverent admiration mixed with a slight sense of your own insignificance.

Now, over-awe takes that feeling and pushes it further — it overwhelms the person so completely that they become silenced, submissive, or incapable of pushing back. The "over-" prefix signals excess. It is awe that has crossed a threshold.
The Full Picture: What Overawe Actually Does to a Person

When someone is overawed, three things tend to happen together:

1. They feel deeply impressed, even humbled. The source of overawing — whether it's a person, an institution, or even a natural force — seems so much greater than them that they feel outmatched.

2. They feel a quiet but real sense of fear or reverence. This is not the same as being terrified. It is a more subtle, respectful kind of fear — the feeling that you dare not challenge or underestimate what's in front of you.

3. They lose the ability to behave normally. An overawed person may go quiet, become timid, hold back their opinions, or simply submit to whoever or whatever is overawing them. Their normal confidence melts away.

This is the key thing to remember: overawe doesn't just impress someone — it disarms them.

Almost anything that carries exceptional power, greatness, or authority:

  • A person of enormous status, fame, or physical presence
  • A mighty institution (a royal court, a supreme court, a powerful army)
  • Extraordinary talent or skill
  • Breathtaking natural scenery (a vast ocean, a towering mountain range)
  • Great wealth or grandeur (a palace, a cathedral)
  • A commanding reputation that precedes someone

"The young lawyer was completely overawed by the Supreme Court judge sitting across from her."
→ She was so overwhelmed by his authority and reputation that she felt nervous, small, and unable to speak confidently.

"Napoleon used the sheer spectacle of his military parades to overawe his enemies before a single shot was fired."
→ He deliberately used display and power to crush the enemy's confidence before battle even began.

"The tourists stood in silence, overawed by the scale of the ancient temple."
→ The temple was so grand and magnificent that they were struck dumb with wonder and reverence.

"He had always overawed his younger siblings, simply by walking into the room."
→ His presence alone was so powerful that it made them feel small and submissive without him even trying.
The Critical Distinction: Overawe vs. Similar Words

Impress vs. Overawe
To impress someone is nice, but it leaves them perfectly functional. You can be impressed by someone and still disagree with them, challenge them, or feel equal to them. To overawe someone is stronger — it leaves them feeling unequal, silenced, or unable to push back. All overawing impresses, but not all impressing overawes.

Intimidate vs. Overawe
Intimidation is mostly about fear and threat — someone makes you afraid they will harm you. Overawe is not primarily about threat. It is about being crushed by greatness, authority, or magnificence — sometimes against your own will. You can be overawed by something beautiful. You cannot really be intimidated by beauty.

Awe vs. Overawe
To "awe" someone fills them with wonder and admiration. To overawe someone does all of that and renders them helpless, submissive, or silent. Overawe is awe with a loss of power attached to it.
How to Use It: Sentence Patterns

Overawe is almost always used in one of two ways:

Active (you are the one causing the feeling):
"Her intelligence overawed everyone in the room."
"The general overawed the enemy with a display of overwhelming force."

Passive (you are the one experiencing the feeling — this is more common):
"He was completely overawed by her presence."
"I felt overawed standing inside the ancient cathedral."
"The new students were overawed by the professor's reputation."

The passive form — "to be overawed by" — is by far the more common pattern you'll encounter in reading and writing.
The Emotional Texture of the Word

Overawe carries a slightly formal, literary weight to it. It is not slang. You would find it in novels, history books, journalism, and serious writing. It describes a genuine psychological state — one where a person, despite possibly wishing to act boldly, finds themselves humbled and quieted by something far greater than themselves.

It is also worth noting that being overawed is not always unpleasant. Sometimes people enjoy being overawed — by a masterpiece painting, by a roaring waterfall, by a legendary performer. The feeling can be sublime. Other times, being overawed is disadvantageous — it costs you your confidence when you need it most.

To overawe someone is to overwhelm them so completely with your power, greatness, or authority that they are left feeling silenced, humbled, and unable to act with their normal confidence.

That is the word — precise, powerful, and a little old-fashioned in the best possible way.
11732:
Overbearing describes a person who is so excessively controlling, domineering, and forceful that they suffocate the freedom, opinions, and comfort of the people around them. An overbearing person acts as though their will, their opinions, and their way of doing things are the only ones that matter — and they push these onto others without caring whether those others agree, feel comfortable, or even want their input.

Think of the word itself for a moment. To "bear down" on something means to press heavily on it, like pressing your thumb onto a surface with force. An overbearing person presses down on those around them — too hard, too much — until those people feel crushed under the weight of their dominance.

An overbearing person tends to show a cluster of behaviors. They:

  • Tell others what to do constantly, even when not asked
  • Override other people's decisions and replace them with their own
  • Dismiss others' opinions as if they're not worth listening to
  • Make people around them feel like they can't think, decide, or speak for themselves
  • Often believe — sincerely — that they know best, and that controlling others is actually helping them

A classic example is a parent who decides everything for their adult child — their career, their relationships, their lifestyle choices — and constantly interferes, corrects, and lectures, even though the child is a fully grown adult who never asked for any of it. That parent is overbearing.

Another example: a boss at work who doesn't just manage their team but micromanages every tiny detail, refuses to listen to employees' ideas, and insists that everything be done exactly their way. That boss is overbearing.
How It Feels to Be Around an Overbearing Person

This is important, because the word carries an emotional weight too. When you're around an overbearing person, you typically feel:

  • Suffocated — like there's no air for your own thoughts or choices
  • Unheard — like your opinion simply doesn't count
  • Pressured — like you must comply or face frustration, criticism, or conflict
  • Small — like your sense of self slowly shrinks around them

The word "overbearing" isn't neutral. It has a distinctly negative tone. When someone is called overbearing, it's a criticism. It means their behavior crosses the line from confident and assertive into oppressive and smothering.
The Key Ingredient: Arrogance Underneath It All

What separates an overbearing person from simply a bossy or strict person is a particular kind of arrogance — an deep-seated belief that they are the authority, that their judgment is superior, and that others should simply fall in line. They often don't see themselves as controlling. In their own mind, they're being helpful, efficient, or responsible. This is part of what makes the trait so frustrating to deal with — you can't easily reason with someone who genuinely believes they're doing you a favor by controlling you.

It's worth being precise about what the word doesn't mean, so you don't confuse it with similar words:

Overbearing ≠ Assertive. An assertive person expresses their opinions and stands their ground confidently — but they still respect that others have their own valid perspectives. An overbearing person doesn't give others that respect.

Overbearing ≠ Strict. A strict teacher has high standards and firm rules. That's not overbearing on its own. Overbearing goes further — it means actively dominating and suppressing others beyond what is fair or reasonable.

Overbearing ≠ Enthusiastic. Someone who is passionate and eager isn't overbearing. The defining mark of overbearing is the force applied against others' freedom or will — not just intensity of personality.
Can It Describe Behavior, Not Just a Person?

Yes. While you most often use it to describe a person ("She is overbearing"), you can also use it to describe someone's manner, tone, or behavior in a specific moment:

  • "His overbearing tone made everyone in the room go silent."
  • "I found her advice well-meaning but overbearing."
  • "The overbearing nature of his management style drove talented people away."

• "My overbearing uncle insisted on planning every detail of the trip, ignoring everything the rest of us wanted."
  • "She meant well, but her overbearing personality made it impossible for her children to develop any independence."
  • "The new manager was so overbearing that half the team put in their resignations within a month."
  • "Living with someone that overbearing is exhausting — you feel like you can never just breathe and be yourself."

If you come across these words, they share the spirit of "overbearing," though each has a slightly different shade:

Domineering is almost a direct synonym — it stresses the desire to dominate and control.
Tyrannical is stronger and darker — it suggests cruelty and oppression, almost like a small dictator.
High-handed means acting with an arrogant disregard for others' feelings or rights.
Imperious carries a similar flavour but with an air of someone acting like royalty — commanding, superior, expecting to be obeyed.
Bossy is the lighter, more informal version — a bossy person likes to give orders, but the word doesn't carry the same depth of suffocation that "overbearing" does.

To fully understand a word, it helps to know what it stands against:

Easygoing — relaxed, not forcing their will on anyone.
Humble — doesn't think themselves superior to others.
Deferential — actively gives way to others' opinions and wishes.
Considerate — thinks about how their actions affect others.
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine someone standing over you, pressing down on your shoulders with both hands, not letting you stand up straight. You can't move freely, you can't be yourself, you can't breathe easily. That's the image the word "overbearing" wants you to feel. The person doing the pressing isn't necessarily evil — they might even think they're helping you stand up properly — but the effect is the same: you are weighed down, controlled, and diminished.

That's overbearing.
11733:
"Overblown" means too much. Something overblown has been puffed up, inflated, or stretched beyond what is true, appropriate, or necessary. The word always signals a gap — a mismatch between what something actually is and how big, serious, grand, or important it is being made to seem.

Think of it like a balloon. Blow it up to the right size and it's fine. Keep blowing past that point and it becomes distorted, fragile, and ridiculous. That's the spirit of "overblown."

1. Exaggerated — bigger in presentation than in reality

This is the most common use. When a situation, claim, reputation, or reaction is described as overblown, it means it has been made to sound far more dramatic, important, or serious than it truly deserves to be.

Examples:

  • "The media coverage of the minor road incident was completely overblown."
    → A small, ordinary event was treated like a major disaster. The coverage didn't match the reality.
  • "His reputation as a genius is overblown — he's smart, but not exceptionally so."
    → People have hyped him up more than reality justifies.
  • "The fears about the new policy turned out to be overblown."
    → People worried far more than the situation actually called for. The danger wasn't as real as imagined.

In all these cases, the word is saying: calm down, it's not as big a deal as you're making it.

2. Pompous and excessive in style — using more grandeur than the situation deserves

When applied to writing, speech, language, or artistic style, "overblown" means unnecessarily extravagant, showy, or self-important. It describes something that is trying too hard to sound impressive and ends up feeling hollow, overdone, or pretentious as a result.

Examples:

  • "The politician's speech was overblown and full of dramatic phrases that said very little."
    → The language was grand and fancy, but the actual content was thin.
  • "The film's overblown musical score made every small moment feel like the end of the world."
    → The music was far too epic and intense for what was happening on screen.
  • "His overblown prose is exhausting to read — three sentences could say what he says in three paragraphs."
    → The writing is needlessly bloated and over-elaborate.

This sense is about style being out of proportion with substance. There's too much decoration, too much drama, too much noise — and not enough real meaning underneath.

In a more literal sense, "overblown" can describe a flower that has bloomed fully and is now past its peak — wilting, fading, overly open. A rose that was beautiful yesterday but is now drooping with petals falling off could be called overblown. This sense appears occasionally in poetry and literary writing, but you will rarely encounter it in everyday conversation.

"Overblown" is almost always critical or dismissive. When you call something overblown, you are essentially saying it doesn't deserve the size, importance, or grandeur that has been given to it. It's a word that deflates things. It pushes back against hype, exaggeration, and pretension.

It is not an extremely harsh word — it's more of a calm, confident correction than an angry attack. Someone who calls a film "overblown" isn't furious; they're unimpressed. They're saying, "All this drama, and for what?"

It's important to separate "overblown" from words that seem similar:

  • Overgrown means something has grown too large physically (like a garden). "Overblown" is about perceived importance or stylistic excess, not physical size.
  • Overthrown means defeated or removed from power (like a government). Completely different.
  • Overrated is close, but specifically means something has received more praise than it deserves. "Overblown" is broader — it can apply to fears, crises, rhetoric, and style, not just praise or reputation.
Common Collocations (Words It Frequently Appears With)

You'll most often see "overblown" paired with words like:

  • overblown rhetoric (language that is too grand and empty)
  • overblown claims (statements that exaggerate the truth)
  • overblown fears / concerns (worries that aren't justified by reality)
  • overblown sense of importance (thinking of yourself or something as far more significant than warranted)
  • overblown production (a film, show, or event that is excessively grand)
  • overblown ego (thinking too highly of yourself)

If you had to summarize "overblown" in one sentence: it describes something that has been given more size, drama, importance, or grandeur than it actually deserves. Whether it's a news story that turned a minor event into a crisis, a speech drowning in fancy words but lacking real ideas, or a reputation that far exceeds someone's actual abilities — if the outside is bigger than the inside, it's overblown.
11734:
Picture yourself on a large ship in the middle of the ocean. The ship has walls on its sides, called railings. If someone slips and falls over those sides and into the water — that's going overboard.

Literally, overboard means: over the side of a ship and into the water.

"The sailor slipped and fell overboard during the storm."
"A huge wave swept the cargo overboard."

In these sentences, overboard answers the question where? — over the edge of the ship, into the sea.
The Figurative Meaning: How the Word Is Actually Used

The literal meaning is rare in daily conversation. The figurative meaning is what you'll hear constantly, and it comes from a simple idea:

Going over the edge of a ship means crossing the boundary of safety — you've gone too far, beyond the limit.

That's exactly what the word means figuratively:

To go overboard = to do something to an excessive degree; to go beyond what is reasonable, necessary, or appropriate.

When someone goes overboard, they don't just do a lot — they do too much. They cross the line.

"She went overboard with the birthday decorations — every wall had streamers, every table had flowers, and there were five cakes for just eight people."

She didn't just decorate. She decorated excessively — more than the situation called for.

"Don't go overboard with the chilli. A small amount is enough."

Don't use too much. Stop before you cross the line.

"I know you're excited, but let's not go overboard — we're working with a small budget."

Let's not do more than is sensible given our situation.

The most important thing to learn about this word is that it almost always appears with the verb go. The phrase "go overboard" is extremely common in English. You will encounter it constantly.

The structure is simple:

  • I went overboard.
  • She's going overboard.
  • Don't go overboard.
  • They went a little overboard.
  • He tends to go overboard with everything.

You can soften it with a little:

"You went a little overboard with the salt, but it's still okay."

Or intensify it with completely or way:

"She completely went overboard planning the wedding — it turned into a year-long project."
"He went way overboard buying gifts. Nobody expected that much."
The Crucial Nuance: It Always Implies Excess

Overboard is never neutral. Every time you use it, you are saying — directly or gently — that someone crossed a line. They did more than they should have.

Sometimes that criticism is harsh:

"The punishment was overboard. The child only made a small mistake."

Sometimes it's affectionate and forgiving:

"You went completely overboard with the gifts! You really didn't have to do all this."

But in both cases, the meaning is the same: a boundary was crossed, more was done than was needed or wise.

This is different from simply saying "a lot." Compare:

  • "She cooked a lot of food." → Neutral. No judgment.
  • "She went overboard cooking food." → She cooked far too much. It was excessive.

The moment you use overboard, you are expressing that a limit was exceeded.

1. "Throw overboard" / "Toss overboard"

This means to completely discard, abandon, or reject something — a plan, an idea, a principle, or even a person.

Just as you might throw unwanted things off a ship into the sea (gone forever), you throw something overboard when you get rid of it entirely, often without much care.

"When the new director arrived, she threw all the existing plans overboard and started from scratch."
→ She completely abandoned the old plans.

"They threw him overboard the moment he became inconvenient."
→ They abandoned him completely when he was no longer useful.

This expression often carries a harsh, cold feeling — it suggests something or someone was discarded without sympathy.

Another common version: "throw caution overboard" — meaning to completely abandon careful, careful thinking and act recklessly.

"He threw caution overboard and spent all his savings on one investment."

2. "Man overboard!"

This is a famous emergency call on ships. When someone shouts "Man overboard!", it means a person has fallen into the sea from the ship and needs immediate rescue. It is a well-known phrase used in its literal sense.

In casual, humorous conversation, people sometimes say "man overboard" to describe a situation where things have gone dramatically wrong.
What Areas of Life Can "Going Overboard" Describe?

The word can describe excess in almost any situation:

Spending money:

"They went overboard on the renovation — what was supposed to cost ₹5 lakhs ended up costing ₹20 lakhs."

Being generous:

"My aunt always goes overboard at Diwali. She sends gifts to every single cousin, even the distant ones she's never met."

Being strict or harsh:

"The manager went overboard with the criticism. One small error doesn't deserve a public scolding in front of the whole team."

Enthusiasm or emotions:

"The fans went overboard when the team won — there were celebrations in the streets for three days."

Using ingredients or products:

"Don't go overboard with the sugar. This recipe only needs a little."
"He went overboard with the cologne. People could smell him before he walked into the room."

Planning or preparing:

"She went overboard preparing for the interview — she had ten different outfits ready and had memorized the company's history going back thirty years."
The Tone and Register of the Word

Overboard is a casual, everyday word. It fits naturally in:

  • Friendly conversations
  • Informal writing
  • Storytelling
  • Advice and suggestions
  • News articles and blogs

It is not a formal or academic word. You wouldn't use it in a legal document or a serious academic paper. But in virtually every other context, it sounds natural and confident.

SenseMeaning

Literal → Over the side of a ship, into the water. ("He fell overboard.")

Figurative (the main use) → To do something excessively, beyond what is reasonable or needed. ("She went overboard with the planning.")

"Go overboard" → The most common phrase. Means to act with too much intensity, spending, effort, emotion, or strictness.

"Throw/toss overboard" → To completely discard or abandon something or someone.

"Man overboard!" → An emergency call meaning someone has fallen into the sea.

Tone → Always implies excess. Never neutral. Can be gently affectionate or sharply critical depending on context.

The heart of this word is simple: the moment you cross the edge of a ship, you've gone too far. That's overboard — in life, in cooking, in spending, in emotions, in anything. It's the point where "enough" became "too much."
11735:
When something or someone is overburdened, it means they are carrying or dealing with far more than they can reasonably handle. The load — whether physical, emotional, or work-related — has crossed a limit. It's not just "a lot"; it's too much, to the point where functioning properly becomes difficult or impossible.

Think of it this way: a donkey can carry a sack of grain. That's a burden. But if you pile on five more sacks, the donkey buckles under the weight. That donkey is now overburdened.

A burden doesn't have to be something physical you carry. It can be:

  • Work or responsibilities — tasks, duties, obligations
  • Emotions — grief, worry, stress, guilt
  • Debt or financial pressure
  • Demand on a system — like too many patients in a hospital

"Overburdened" simply means the burden, in whichever form it takes, has exceeded what can be reasonably managed.
The key implication: strain and impairment

This is what makes "overburdened" precise and powerful. It doesn't just mean "busy" or "full." It means the load has caused a breakdown in normal functioning. Something is suffering because of the excess. A person who is overburdened isn't just tired — they are struggling to keep up, things are slipping, and they likely need relief.

This is important: overburdened implies the limit has already been crossed, not just approached.
How it's used — the three main contexts

1. People (emotionally or professionally)

"After her mother fell ill, she was overburdened with caretaking responsibilities alongside her full-time job."

"The young teacher felt overburdened — she had 45 students, no assistant, and mountains of paperwork."

Here, "overburdened" tells you the person is under a crushing weight of duties or feelings, more than one person should be expected to handle alone.

2. Systems and institutions

"The public healthcare system is overburdened, with patients waiting weeks for basic care."

"An overburdened court system means cases drag on for years."

When we call a system overburdened, we mean it is receiving more demand than it was designed or has the capacity to handle. Quality and efficiency drop as a result.

3. Physical things (less common but correct)

"The overburdened bridge finally collapsed under the weight of the trucks."

"An overburdened shelf groaned under the weight of the books."

This is the most literal use — an object carrying more physical weight than it can structurally support.
The emotional tone: sympathy, not criticism

"Overburdened" almost always carries a tone of sympathy. When you describe someone as overburdened, you are saying the situation is unfair or unreasonable — they have been given or ended up with too much through no fault of their own. It is not a criticism of the person; it is a criticism of the load placed upon them.

Compare:

  • "She is overburdened." → She has too much to deal with; the situation is unfair.
  • "She is incompetent." → She can't handle things; the fault lies with her.

Very different. "Overburdened" places the problem on the amount of burden, not the person's ability.
How it differs from similar words

Overwhelmed — very close in meaning, but "overwhelmed" tends to focus more on the emotional and psychological state (feeling flooded, unable to think clearly). "Overburdened" focuses more on the quantity of load — the pile of things itself. An overwhelmed person may freeze; an overburdened person is likely still struggling along, but straining.

Overloaded — similar, but more commonly used for things, systems, or technical contexts (an overloaded circuit, an overloaded server). "Overburdened" sounds more human and empathetic.

Swamped — informal and casual. You'd say "I'm swamped with emails" in conversation. "Overburdened" is more formal and carries more gravity.

Stretched thin — means having too many responsibilities spread across too few resources (time, energy, people). It's close, but "overburdened" is stronger — it implies the weight is actually causing harm, not just making things tight.
A few more example sentences to cement it

"Doctors in the public sector are overburdened, often seeing 80 patients a day."

"He was emotionally overburdened after losing his job and going through a divorce at the same time."

"The overburdened infrastructure of the city could not handle the growing population."

"New teachers are often overburdened with administrative work that leaves little time for actual teaching."

"Relief workers in the disaster zone were completely overburdened — too few people, too many needs."

Overburdened means: carrying or dealing with more than can be reasonably or properly handled. It applies to people, systems, and physical things. It always implies that a limit has been crossed, that there is strain or impairment as a result, and it carries a tone of sympathy toward whoever or whatever is overburdened. The word is formal in register and particularly common in discussions of social issues — healthcare, education, infrastructure, justice systems — wherever demand has outpaced capacity.
11736:
When we say the sky is overcast, we mean it is completely — or almost completely — covered by a thick blanket of clouds. The clouds spread across the entire sky, hiding the sun and turning everything a dull shade of grey.

Think of it this way: on a sunny day, you look up and see blue sky with maybe a few white clouds drifting here and there. On an overcast day, those clouds have multiplied and merged together into one large, unbroken grey sheet that covers everything above you. There is no blue sky visible, no bright sun — just a uniform grey ceiling of cloud.
What an overcast day actually feels like

On an overcast day:

  • The light is dim and flat — everything looks a little duller than usual, like someone turned the brightness down on the world.
  • There are no sharp shadows, because there is no direct sunlight hitting objects.
  • It often feels cooler than a sunny day, because the clouds block the warmth of the sun.
  • It can feel gloomy or heavy, though it does not necessarily mean rain is coming (though it might).

An overcast sky is not the same as a stormy, dramatic sky with dark thunderclouds. It is more like a quiet, grey, heavy stillness overhead.

This is important to get right, because several words feel similar but mean different things.

Cloudy vs. overcast:
"Cloudy" is a broader, more flexible word. A cloudy sky can have some clouds mixed with patches of blue sky and sunshine. Overcast is stronger — it means the clouds have taken over the entire sky. No gaps, no blue, no sun. Every overcast sky is cloudy, but not every cloudy sky is overcast.

Foggy vs. overcast:
Fog is a low-lying mist that sits close to the ground, making it hard to see things at a distance. Overcast is specifically about the sky above you being covered in clouds. A day can be both foggy and overcast, but they describe two separate things.

Gloomy vs. overcast:
"Gloomy" is more of a feeling — a general sense of darkness, sadness, or bleakness. "Overcast" is a factual, objective description of what the sky looks like. However, an overcast day often causes a gloomy feeling, which is why the two words are often used together.

Grey vs. overcast:
"Grey" simply describes the colour. "Overcast" explains why it looks grey — because the clouds are covering the sky.

Not all overcast skies are identical. The word can describe a range:

  • Lightly overcast: A thin, pale layer of cloud covers the sky. Some soft light still filters through. You might be able to faintly make out where the sun is hiding behind the clouds.
  • Heavily overcast / completely overcast: A thick, dense layer of cloud. Very little light gets through. The sky looks dark grey or even charcoal-coloured. This kind of sky often brings rain.

In weather reports and forecasts, "overcast" typically signals that cloud cover is at or close to 100% — meteorologists use it when clouds cover at least 7/8ths of the sky.
How to use it in sentences

Here are natural, realistic example sentences so you can see how this word sits in real life:

  • "The sky was completely overcast, and we couldn't find a single patch of blue."
  • "It was an overcast morning — grey clouds stretched all the way to the horizon."
  • "Despite the overcast skies, it didn't actually rain."
  • "Photographers sometimes prefer overcast days because the soft, even light creates no harsh shadows."
  • "We had planned a picnic, but the overcast weather made us change our minds."

Like many weather words in English, "overcast" sometimes travels beyond the weather and is used figuratively — meaning it is applied to emotions, moods, or situations to suggest darkness, heaviness, or gloom.

  • "His face was overcast with worry." — His expression looked troubled and dark, the way a grey sky looks.
  • "The sad news cast an overcast shadow over the celebration." — The happiness of the event was dimmed and weighed down, the way clouds dim a bright day.

This figurative use is less common than the weather meaning, but you will encounter it in literature, poetry, and sometimes in everyday speech.

You will often see or hear "overcast" used alongside:

  • sky — overcast sky
  • day — an overcast day
  • morning / afternoon / evening — an overcast morning
  • weather — overcast weather
  • conditions — overcast conditions (often used in weather forecasts or news reports)
  • heavily / completely / partly — these adverbs tell you how much of the sky is covered
One-sentence summary to anchor it all

Overcast means: the sky is fully covered by clouds, blocking the sun and turning everything a dull, flat grey.

Everything else you've read above is just the layers of detail that surround and sharpen that core idea.
11737:
To understand "overdue," you first need to understand the word "due."

When something is due, it means it is expected, required, or supposed to happen at a particular time. A deadline has been set. For example, a rent payment "due on the 1st of every month" means you are expected to pay your rent on the 1st.

Now, "over" here means beyond or past.

So, overdue = something that was supposed to happen by a certain time, but that time has already passed, and it still has not happened.

The two key ingredients are:

  1. A deadline or expected time existed.
  2. That deadline has passed, yet the thing is still not done, not paid, not returned, or not delivered.

The moment the thing finally happens — the moment the bill is paid, the book is returned, the baby is born — it is no longer overdue.
The two main ways "overdue" is used

Way 1: A specific deadline was missed (and the thing is still pending)

This is the most common and concrete use of the word. There was a clear deadline, that deadline has passed, and the expected thing has not happened yet.

  • "Your electricity bill is overdue."

— The bill had a payment deadline (say, October 15th). That date has passed. You still haven't paid it. Until you pay it, it remains overdue.

  • "The library book is overdue."

— The book was supposed to be returned by a certain date. That date has passed, and the book is still with you.

  • "The package is overdue."

— The package was supposed to arrive by Tuesday. It's now Thursday, and it still hasn't come.

  • "She is three weeks overdue." (said about a pregnant woman)

— Her baby was expected to be born three weeks ago (based on the due date), but the baby hasn't been born yet.

In all these cases, there is a concrete deadline that was set in advance, and that deadline has clearly been missed.

Way 2: Something should have happened sooner (a judgment, not a fixed deadline)

This is a softer, more evaluative use of "overdue." Here, no specific deadline was officially set — but people feel that something should have happened much earlier than it did (or still hasn't happened and should have). The word expresses that something is needed, deserved, or right, and that it has been delayed longer than it should have.

  • "This road has needed repair for years. The renovation is long overdue."

— There was no official repair deadline, but everyone agrees the road should have been fixed a long time ago.

  • "She has been working incredibly hard for five years. A promotion is overdue."

— No one set a formal deadline for her promotion, but the speaker believes she deserved to be promoted before now.

  • "An apology from him is overdue."

— He should have apologized earlier; he hasn't yet.

  • "These reforms are long overdue."

— The changes needed to happen earlier; people feel they've been waiting too long.

The phrase "long overdue" is especially common in this second sense, and it emphasizes that something should have happened much earlier than now.

You will often see "overdue for" followed by a noun. This means a person or thing has gone too long without something happening to them, and it's time for it to happen.

  • "I'm overdue for a haircut." — I should have gotten a haircut earlier; I've waited too long.
  • "The car is overdue for a service." — The car should have been serviced by now; it's been too long.
  • "He's overdue for some good luck." — He's had a streak of bad luck for too long; good luck is expected to come his way.

This is an important distinction.

"Late" simply means something happened after the expected time — but it may have already happened. "Late" tells you when something happened.

  • "The train arrived late." → The train did eventually arrive, but it arrived after the scheduled time.
  • "He submitted the report late." → The report has been submitted, but it was submitted after the deadline.

"Overdue" means something has not yet happened even though the deadline has already passed. It refers to something that is still pending.

  • "The train is overdue." → The train was expected at 9 AM. It's now 9:30 AM. The train still has not arrived.
  • "The report is overdue." → The report was due yesterday. It still has not been submitted.

In short: "late" describes timing (it happened, but after the expected time). "Overdue" describes a current state of something still not having happened (the deadline is gone, and we're still waiting).

• It does not describe a person who was late to arrive somewhere. You would not say, "He was overdue to the meeting." You'd say, "He was late to the meeting." Overdue refers to things like payments, events, deliveries, or actions — not to people being punctual.
  • It does not mean something is unlikely to happen. It means something should have already happened.
A quick summary to lock it in

Overdue describes something that was expected or required by a certain point in time, but has not yet happened even though that time has passed.

It can be used literally (a missed bill, a library book not returned, a delayed baby) or evaluatively (a change that should have happened sooner, recognition that someone deserves). Either way, the core idea is always the same: the clock ran out, and we're still waiting.
11738:
To overegg the pudding means to overdo something — to add more than is needed, usually to make something seem better, more impressive, or more dramatic than it really is. The result of this "overdoing" is that things actually get worse, not better. The exaggeration becomes obvious, and people stop believing you or taking you seriously.

Think of it this way: it means trying too hard to improve something, and in doing so, ruining it.

The idiom comes straight from the kitchen — specifically, from British cooking.

In British cuisine, a "pudding" isn't just what Americans call pudding (a creamy dessert). It's a broader term for many kinds of baked or steamed dishes, both sweet (like a sponge pudding) and savoury. Eggs are a critical ingredient in these recipes. They bind the ingredients together and give the pudding its texture — light, airy, and just right.

Now, here's the key: eggs only work well in the right amount. If you add the correct number of eggs, your pudding comes out perfectly. But if you think, "More eggs = better pudding," and you start cracking in extra eggs, something goes wrong. The pudding becomes rubbery, heavy, and unpleasant. Your good intention has backfired completely. You tried to make it better, but you made it worse.

That is the heart of this idiom. Just as adding too many eggs ruins a pudding, overdoing anything — especially exaggerating or over-embellishing — ruins the thing you're trying to improve.
The Key Idea: It Always Backfires

This is the most important nuance to understand: overegging the pudding doesn't just mean adding extra — it means the extra addition causes harm. The excess defeats the purpose.

This is what separates this idiom from simply saying "too much." It specifically implies:

  1. You were trying to enhance or improve something.
  2. You went beyond what was needed.
  3. Because of that excess, the result is now less convincing, less effective, or less believable.

The idiom is flexible. You can overegg the pudding in many different situations:

  • Exaggerating a story — You add so many dramatic details that people roll their eyes and don't believe the core truth anymore.
  • Over-praising something — You describe a product, person, or event in such glowing terms that it sounds fake and untrustworthy.
  • Over-decorating or over-designing — You add so many features, colours, or elements that the end result looks cluttered and messy.
  • Making an argument too forcefully — You pile on so many points, so many statistics, and so much emotion that your argument feels desperate rather than convincing.
  • Over-acting — A performer exaggerates their expressions and gestures so much that the audience laughs instead of feeling moved.

In every case, the person's effort to strengthen something has weakened it instead.

Here are examples to see how the idiom works in sentences:

  • "His speech was good, but he overegged the pudding by repeating the same point five times. People started getting bored."
    → He made the speech longer and more forceful than it needed to be, and it hurt rather than helped.
  • "The advertisement overegged the pudding — calling a basic smartphone 'the most revolutionary device in human history' just made people laugh."
    → The exaggerated praise destroyed the ad's credibility.
  • "She overegged the pudding on her CV by listing skills she barely had. When the interviewer asked about them, she was embarrassed."
    → Embellishing her qualifications beyond reality backfired badly.
  • "The cake was already delicious. Adding three layers of extra frosting was overegging the pudding — now it's sickly sweet."
    → A literal near-example. Something already good was made worse by unnecessary additions.
  • "The film's ending was emotional, but the director overegged the pudding with that ten-minute crying scene. It went from moving to melodramatic."
    → Too much emotional intensity undermined the very emotion the director was aiming for.
A Subtle but Important Point: Intention vs. Result

Notice that when someone overeggs the pudding, their intention is usually good. They want to:

  • Make their story more interesting.
  • Make their product sound more appealing.
  • Make their argument more persuasive.

They are not lying for the sake of lying. They genuinely believe that "more" will help. But because they misjudge how much is "too much," the result is the opposite of what they hoped for. This is why the idiom often carries a slightly sympathetic but also critical tone — it's a gentle or pointed way of saying, "You tried too hard, and it didn't work."
Tone and Register: When Do People Use It?

This idiom is informal, but not slang. It sits comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Journalism and opinion writing
  • Politics (it's particularly popular among British politicians and commentators)
  • Reviews of films, books, restaurants, or performances

It is predominantly British English. If you say it to an American, they may not immediately understand it. An equivalent American expression would be something like "laying it on too thick" or "gilding the lily" (though these have slightly different flavours, explained below).
How Is It Different From Similar Expressions?

"Laying it on thick" — This means flattering someone excessively or being overly complimentary, often to manipulate them. It's more focused on praise and flattery specifically. "Overegging the pudding" is broader — it applies to any kind of excess, not just flattery.

"Gilding the lily" — This means adding unnecessary decoration or improvement to something that is already perfect. The difference is subtle but real: gilding the lily is about doing something pointless (the lily is already beautiful; gold paint is unnecessary but doesn't necessarily make it ugly). Overegging the pudding is about doing something that actively makes things worse. One is wasteful; the other is counterproductive.

"Going overboard" — This means doing too much of something in a general sense. It's less specific about the idea that the excess harms credibility or quality. "Overegging the pudding" has that specific sense of undermining the thing you're trying to strengthen.
A Quick Formula to Remember It

If you want a mental shortcut, remember this:

Overegging the pudding = Well-intentioned excess + Backfiring result

You tried to make something better. You added too much. Now it's worse — and probably less believable.

"Overegg the pudding" means to exaggerate or overdo something so much — in an attempt to make it better — that you actually make it worse, often by making it seem unbelievable, excessive, or ridiculous.
11739:
To overestimate something means to think it is more than it actually is — bigger, stronger, better, longer, harder, or more important than it truly is in reality.

The word has two parts that tell you exactly what it means:

  • "Over" = too much, beyond what is correct
  • "Estimate" = to form a judgment or rough calculation about something

Put them together: to estimate too high. To believe something is more than it really is.

You can overestimate almost anything — a number, a distance, a person's skill, the importance of something, how much time something takes, how much food you need, and so on.

Here are some everyday examples:

  • Overestimating a quantity:

"I overestimated how much rice we'd need. I cooked for ten people, but only four came."
(You thought the amount needed was more than it actually was.)

  • Overestimating time:

"She overestimated how long the journey would take. She thought it would be three hours, but it was only ninety minutes."
(She thought it would take longer than it did.)

  • Overestimating difficulty:

"He overestimated how hard the exam would be. He studied for two full weeks and finished the paper in forty minutes."
(He believed it was harder than it turned out to be.)

  • Overestimating importance:

"Don't overestimate the impact of one bad presentation. It won't ruin your career."
(Don't think that one mistake matters more than it really does.)

  • Overestimating distance:

"I overestimated how far the shop was. It's just around the corner!"
(I thought it was farther away than it is.)

You can also overestimate a person's abilities, strength, knowledge, or character.

  • "The manager overestimated Ravi's experience and gave him a project he wasn't ready for."

(The manager thought Ravi was more capable than he actually was at that point.)

  • "Don't overestimate your opponent. They may surprise you."

(Don't assume they are better or more dangerous than they really are — but ironically, this also means: be careful not to *underestimate them either.)*

  • "He tends to overestimate himself."

(He thinks too highly of his own abilities. He believes he's better at things than he really is.)

This last use — overestimating yourself — is very common. It means having an inflated idea of your own skills, knowledge, or strength.

There are two phrases in English that look similar but mean very different things. This confuses many people, so pay attention:

"It is easy to overestimate X"
→ People often make the mistake of thinking X is more/greater than it is.
→ Example: "It is easy to overestimate how much influence social media has on our daily decisions."
(In reality, that influence may be smaller than people think.)

"It is hard to overestimate X" (or "It is difficult to overestimate X")
→ X is SO great or so important that even if you think very highly of it, you probably still haven't given it enough credit. The real value is that high.
→ Example: "It is hard to overestimate the importance of sleep for your health."
(Sleep is so critical that you almost can't exaggerate how important it is — your highest estimate is probably still not high enough.)

These two phrases are essentially opposites in meaning, even though they look alike. "Easy to overestimate" = people think too highly of it. "Hard to overestimate" = it deserves even more credit than people give it.

People sometimes confuse overestimate with exaggerate. They are related but not the same.

  • Exaggerate often means to deliberately or expressively describe something as bigger or more extreme than it is — sometimes for effect, humor, or drama. "I've told you a million times!" — that's an exaggeration. Nobody literally said something a million times.
  • Overestimate is more about a genuine misjudgment or incorrect calculation. When you overestimate, you actually believe something is more than it is — you're not just saying it for effect. It's a mistake in your thinking or judgment, not a dramatic flourish.

That said, in casual speech, people sometimes use them loosely and interchangeably.

The natural opposite of overestimate is underestimate — to think something is less than it actually is.

  • Overestimate: You think it's more than it is. → You overprepare, overreact, or set expectations too high.
  • Underestimate: You think it's less than it is. → You underprepare, get caught off guard, or undervalue something.

Knowing both words together makes each of them clearer.

Overestimating isn't always harmless. It can lead to:

  • Poor decisions — If you overestimate your savings, you might spend more than you should.
  • Disappointment — If you overestimate how good a movie will be, you'll likely walk out disappointed.
  • Wasted effort — If you overestimate how hard a task is, you might over-prepare and waste time.
  • Conflict — If a business overestimates demand, it produces too much and loses money.
  • Misjudging people — If you overestimate someone's loyalty, you might trust them more than they deserve.

Sometimes, though, a small overestimation is harmless or even useful — for example, overestimating how long a trip will take means you'll leave early and arrive on time.

To overestimate = to judge something as being more (larger, stronger, better, longer, harder, more important) than it really is.

It can be about numbers, time, distance, importance, difficulty, or a person's ability (including your own). It usually implies a mistake in judgment — a gap between what you thought and what actually is. The result is often that your expectations don't match reality.
